newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian bonds fired up again on U.S. surge.
newsitem.headline: Australian bonds fired up again on U.S. surge.

text.p: *Australian bonds put aside their recent concerns over an ailing local dollar and rallied strongly with U.S. Treasuries to set fresh 3-1/2 year yield lows at the long end.
*U.S. yields dive on small 0.1 percent June CPI rise.
The Australian bond market put aside its recent concerns over an ailing local dollar and rallied strongly with U.S. Treasuries on a modest U.S. CPI rise.

The September 10-year bond futures struck a fresh 3-1/2 year of 93.440 high just after the opening, taking out the peak of 93.430 seen in after hours trade, and continuing the solid rebound from Wednesday's 93.235 low.

"The market's looking in better shape after yesterday's shake-out. It's looking less likely that the Fed will tighten, and I think we will probably be testing 93.500 going into next week's (Australian) CPI," one trader said.
The U.S. 30-year bond yield dropped to 6.58 percent, its lowest level since December 1996, after its CPI rose just 0.1 percent for an annual rate of 2.3 percent.
While U.S. analysts raved about their inflation record, Australia will be looking to outdo this performance once again when the second quarter CPI is released next Wednesday.

A recent Reuters poll of economists expected headine inflation to be flat on the quarter for an annual rate of a mere 0.6 percent, while the policy sensitive underlying rate is seen up 0.4 percent for annual growth of 1.7 percent. This would be below the Reserve Bank's 2.0-3.0 percent target.
Such outcomes are expected to see a further contraction in yield differentials to the U.S. and a continued move towards parity on the 10-year spread, currently around 40 basis points.
"The local market has got a lot of good news built in, but I wouldn't be surprised to see the spread in the 20 to 25 (basis point) area after the CPI," one trader said.

Meanwhile, the Australian dollar saw a meagre rebound from Wednesday's weak local close of US$0.7325/30. The risk of a monetary policy easing continues to weigh on the unit, which for the debt market, has cast some doubts over whether the RBA would carry out such a move and threaten further currency weakness.

The local market slightly outperformed the long end of the U.S. curve. However, it dragged its heels against the rest of the bloc, particularly against New Zealand, which rebounded strongly after Wednesday's weak performance. N.Z. retail sales fell a larger than expected 4.6 percent in May.
